title: Less business (Avot 4:10)
hook: a calendar with no white space left: Meir says lessen business, busy yourself with Torah, be humble before everyone
tomorrow: who speaks up for you in a room you're not in?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbi Yonatan: keep it in a thin week and you'll keep it in a full one. Poor or rich. Now, the week that's too full.
screen: `POOR OR RICH.` → `THE WEEK THAT'S TOO FULL.`

segments.voice: Color-coded blocks from seven in the morning to ten at night, and a meeting about the other meetings. Too busy to breathe. Rabbi Meir has a three-part answer, and the first part is blunt: do less business. Lessen your dealings, busy yourself with Torah, and be humble before every person. But another sage in the same book would push back on that first part. So today, two voices.
screen: `NO WHITE SPACE LEFT.` → `RABBI MEIR: DO LESS BUSINESS.` → `ANOTHER SAGE PUSHES BACK.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Meir first. Lessen your business and busy yourself with Torah. He goes on: if you neglect the Torah, many reasons to neglect it will line up in front of you. His best case is that busyness multiplies. Every task breeds two more, and there's never a natural gap where the important thing fits. So you have to cut on purpose, or the Torah gets the leftovers, which is nothing. Now the other voice. Back in chapter two, Rabban Gamliel, son of Rabbi Yehudah the Prince, says Torah study is beautiful together with an honest living, because the effort of both keeps you from wrongdoing. Study with no work, he warns, comes to nothing in the end. His best case is that work isn't the enemy of a holy life. A trade keeps you honest, fed, and in the world, and learning that floats free of it can go wrong. Notice what the two don't disagree about. Neither says quit your job. Neither says skip the learning. The argument is about the default: does work get trimmed to make room, or does learning ride alongside a full day? Avot keeps both voices in the same book and doesn't pick a winner. And Rabbi Meir's third part fits either one. Be humble before every person. A full calendar can make anyone feel important. Less business starts with one cut.
screen: `MEIR: CUT, OR TORAH GETS LEFTOVERS.` · `GAMLIEL: TORAH WITH A LIVING.` · `NEITHER SAYS QUIT. NEITHER SAYS SKIP.` · `BE HUMBLE BEFORE EVERY PERSON.` · then, large: `LESS BUSINESS.`

segments.voice: Open your calendar or your list, and find one thing this week you could drop, shorten, or hand back without anyone being hurt. Cross it off or delete it now, as one small act. Then, for the rest of the sit, let the space it leaves stay empty.
screen: `FIND ONE BUSYNESS.` · `DROP IT NOW.` · `LET THE SPACE STAY EMPTY.`

segments.voice: Less business. Rabbi Meir's advice: lessen your dealings and busy yourself with Torah, or the reasons not to will multiply.
Pocket this: less business, one cut at a time, with both sages listening. Day thirty-two of the rest of Avot.

howItsDone: Many working Jews set a short fixed time for study inside a full day, before work, at lunch, or in a class after evening prayers, while others set aside longer stretches by cutting back on other commitments.

myth: Rabbi Meir tells people to quit their jobs and only study

fork.setup: your friend picks up a third after-school job and drops the weekly study group she loves, saying it'll come back when things calm down. you make Rabbi Meir's case first. now make Rabban Gamliel's best case. which is it?
options: an honest living isn't the enemy of learning; keep both, even if the study gets smaller.
work matters more than study, so the study group can simply wait for later.
busyness always multiplies, so she should drop the jobs and only study.
fork.reveal: Gamliel praises Torah together with a living. the second option drops the Torah, which neither sage does; the third is Meir's view overstated into quitting.

original.note: Hebrew: be one who lessens business. esek is dealings, the busyness of trade.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old line against working too hard.
what it means: cut on purpose, or busyness multiplies and the Torah gets the leftovers; and stay humble before every person.
what a scholar hears: Avot keeps a real tension, Meir's 'lessen business' beside Rabban Gamliel's Torah with derech eretz in 2:2, and the Talmud keeps arguing it.
guess: cut back your dealings to make room for Torah
run your business honestly and keep fair scales
do business only with people of your own faith
recall: keep it in want, keep it in plenty
God alone judges alone; people consult

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 (recipe v3): debate shape. Two views inside the tradition: Rabbi Meir (4:10, lessen business) and Rabban Gamliel son of Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi (2:2, Torah with derech eretz is beautiful; Torah without work ends in nothing and brings sin). Both paraphrased. The voice says Avot 'doesn't pick a winner'; confirm that is fair (Gamliel's line is about combining, Meir's about reducing; they aren't strict opposites).

Trapdoor mentions the Talmud keeps arguing it (Berakhot 35b, Rabbi Yishmael vs Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai) without detail; confirm or cut.
